newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: German exodus from Kazakhstan unwanted, Bonn says.
newsitem.headline: German exodus from Kazakhstan unwanted, Bonn says.

text.p: A senior German official said on Wednesday Kazakhstan's many ethnic Germans should not deceive themselves over life in Germany, their historic motherland, and the Kazakh government should continue reforms to stop emigration.

"Several hundred thousand Germans live today in Kazakhstan, representing a good opportunity for future relations between our countries," Carl-Dieter Spranger, Germany's Minister of Economic Cooperation and Development, told a news conference.

But Spranger, who spent a day with officials in the former Soviet republic discussing a set of issues including the German community, added: "Neither Germany nor Kazakhstan want a larger number of Germans living here to emigrate to Germany."

In the Soviet Union's last census in 1989, 1.1 million of Kazakhstan's 16.7 million citizens described themselves as Germans. But subsequent mass emigration to Germany, caused mainly by severe economic problems, means that less than 400,000 remain.
The Kazakh Germans are mostly descendants of Germans deported to the region during World war Two by Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin.
Many are disillusioned with life in Kazakhstan and last year alone 92,000 left for Germany after proving their German origin and passing compulsory language tests.
But Spranger warned Kazakhstan's German community against illusions of carefree life in Germany, which itself has a number of acute problems.
"We have now 4.3 million of unemployed. The prospects for immigrants are also not the best, and one should have no illusions about one's future in Germany," he said.
The minister stressed that there was no discrimination against Germans in Kazakhstan.

He said that during his meetings with senior officials of the Kazakh government he insisted that the Central Asian state proceed with its radical reforms to make the transition to a market-based economy less painful.
"The general economic situation in the country must improve to give everyone the chance to live here in better conditions and not to leave the country," he said.

Spranger said Germany had allotted 55 million marks to ethnic Germans living in Kazakhstan, but did not elaborate on how the money was spent. Bonn would work to develop small and medium-sized business with Kazakhstan, he added.

Annual emigration of ethnic Germans from the Commonwealth of Independent States was below the annual 200,000 limit set by Bonn last year. But the German government is nevertheless anxious to stem the tide from the former Soviet Union.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who visited Kazakhstan earlier this month, said he agreed with Kazakh President Nursulatan Nazarbayev that joint German-Kazakh businesses would be developed mainly in regions populated by ethnic Germans.
